Does Excluding Others Strengthen One’s Own Position?!— On the Hefazat Ameer’s Declaration Regarding the Saad-Affiliated Tabligh Group

I came across a report on Facebook stating that the respected Ameer of Hefazat-e-Islam has declared: “The Saad-affiliated faction of Tabligh Jamaat will never again be allowed to use the Tongi Biswa Ijtema grounds.”

Without knowing the full context or the precise circumstances surrounding this statement, I do not wish to blame anyone. Nevertheless, the matter raises several questions of principle that deserve careful consideration.

I am offering these reflections not as a supporter or opponent of either side, but from the perspective of a third party. Some may ask: Who am I to comment on this matter? My humble response is that, although I am not directly associated with Tabligh Jamaat, I acknowledge its positive contributions to the service of Islam. Therefore, whenever I witness disputes, divisions, or mutual confrontations within the movement, I feel personally distressed.

It is out of this sense of responsibility and goodwill that I wish to share a few thoughts—not to demean either side or endorse the position of the other, but to encourage the resolution of mutual disputes, fair treatment, and consideration of the broader interests of the dīn.

The longstanding dispute and division between the two factions of Tabligh Jamaat are undoubtedly undesirable and deeply regrettable. It is painful to see such distance and discord between people who once shared meals at the same table and taught others the values of brotherhood, ikhlāṣ, and mutual affection.

Differences of opinion and organisational divisions, however, are not unusual. Even biological brothers may disagree and fall into conflict. But such disagreements do not entitle one side to undermine the legitimate rights or dignity of the other. Differences may give rise to disputes, but they cannot serve as a justification for depriving anyone of their rights.

In this situation, one option worth considering would have been to arrange separate Ijtema gatherings for the two factions at different times, ensuring that neither side faced unnecessary inconvenience or embarrassment because of the other. If administrative or legal constraints existed, solutions could have been explored through discussions with the relevant authorities.

If such a conciliatory arrangement were feasible, would it not offer a more practical and peaceful solution than declaring that one side would be completely excluded?!

When a group is excluded entirely from a particular space simply because its views or methods of propagation are disliked, the result may be to deepen and complicate the dispute rather than resolve it. Such measures may even widen the existing distance and distrust between the two sides, intensifying mutual hostility. Consequently, a disagreement that could potentially be settled through dialogue may develop into a prolonged conflict.

In a diverse and democratic society, the appropriate way to address differences of opinion is not coercion, but reasoned argument, dialogue, mutual tolerance, and lawful procedures. You may propagate your own views, while the other side should also have the opportunity to present its position. If you consider someone’s arguments mistaken, you should respond with reason and evidence and, where necessary, pursue the appropriate organisational and legal processes. If any party engages in unlawful activities, the remedy must likewise be sought through lawful means. A unilateral declaration or a display of power cannot substitute for a just resolution of a dispute.

Another issue deserves particular attention here.

When responsible religious leaders speak without sufficient balance, restraint, or foresight, their words can adversely influence the attitudes and behaviour of their followers. In particular, if a statement encourages hostility, intolerance, or confrontation among followers, its undesirable consequences may extend beyond the organisation concerned and affect the wider community of ʿulamāʾ. It may also foster negative perceptions of religious scholars among the general public.

Those from whom society expects lessons in restraint, tolerance, and justice have an even greater responsibility to reflect these values in their words and conduct. The statements of people in positions of responsibility do not merely express their personal views; they can also shape the attitudes and behaviour of their followers. Therefore, considering the possible social consequences of a statement before making it is itself an essential part of leadership.

The Qawmi sphere is already facing numerous internal problems, differences of opinion, and organisational challenges.

Under these circumstances, what is the point of creating new grounds for conflict instead of taking the initiative to resolve existing disputes? Differences of opinion are inevitable, but why must every disagreement be turned into a confrontation?

If, in attempting to counter opposing views, we disregard the very principles of mutual rights, coexistence, and brotherhood, what message are we conveying to our followers? Before calling upon others to reform themselves, should we not set an example of the same principles of justice and restraint when resolving our own disputes?

The responsibility of the ʿulamāʾ is not limited to speaking about the dīn; they must also exemplify justice, tolerance, discipline, and brotherhood through their own conduct. If these principles are disregarded in disputes among themselves, both the credibility and the moral influence of their message may come under question in the eyes of society.

It is worth remembering that one may establish one’s position by belittling others, but doing so does not establish the moral superiority of that position.

**Our expectation is that the responsible individuals concerned will consider this matter by rising above partisan or organisational interests and viewing it instead through the lens of the broader interests of the dīn, mutual rights, and social harmony.**
